title: In-Situ Atomic-Scale Visualization of Dual Oxidation Mechanisms in NiCr Alloys
content: Nickel-chromium (NiCr) alloys are indispensable in high-temperature applications due to their excellent resistance to oxidation and corrosion. When exposed to oxidizing environments, Cr within the alloy reacts with oxygen to form a stable and adherent Cr oxide (Cr2O3) surface layer [1, 2]. This Cr-rich oxide scale acts as a self-limiting barrier, blocking the inward diffusion of oxygen and other corrosive species (e.g., S, C) while suppressing outward metal ion migration, thereby preventing the underlying alloy from further degradation. The long-term performance of NiCr alloys in extreme environments hinges on the integrity and continuity of this Cr2O3layer, which mitigates diverse forms of high-temperature corrosion [3, 4], including carburization, sulfidation, and oxidation. Paradoxically, while the protective role of Cr2O3 is well-established, the initial stages of oxidation—particularly the atomic-scale mechanisms governing oxide nucleation, competitive growth between Cr2O3 and NiO, and early microstructural evolution—remain poorly resolved. Key uncertainties persist regarding how local compositional gradients, interfacial stresses, crystal facets, and defect dynamics influence the transition from transient oxide formation to a continuous Cr2O3 scale. This knowledge gap obstructs efforts to rationally design NiCr alloys with enhanced durability, as microstructural heterogeneities in the oxide layer (e.g., porosity, cracking) directly compromise its protective function under cyclic thermal and chemical loads.
